newsitem.title: BURUNDI: African sanctions team meets Burundi leaders.
newsitem.headline: African sanctions team meets Burundi leaders.

text.p: A delegation from regional countries that have imposed sanctions on Burundi said their first direct talks with military ruler Major Pierre Buyoya were useful.

It was the first time a delegation had visited and toured the capital Bujumbura since regional African presidents imposed sanctions six days after a bloodless coup that brought Buyoya to power on July 25.
Diplomats and aid workers said the visit by East African ministers could break a deadlock over the conditions for regional states to lift the economic and transport embargo.

The delegation was led by Tanzania's foreign minister Jakaya Kikwete and had more than two hours of talks with Buyoya and Hutu Prime Minister Pascal Firmin Ndimira to say the discussions were positive but no deals had been struck.
The meeting served as a first step to further discussions with Burundi's government, delegation members said.
"We have had a useful encounter and we think there will be forward movement," Kikwete said.
The ministers stood by the results of the latest regional summit, at which it was decided to maintain an economic and transport embargo, Burundi Foreign Minister Luc Rukingama said.
Buyoya argued the embargo should be lifted and restated that talks between the government and Hutu rebels could not take place while the blockade remained, Rukingama added.

"Almost all the conditions have been fulfilled and it is only logical to lift sanctions. It would be very difficult to engage in dialogue when children are being killed and the population is starving," Rukingama told reporters.
"But they came to talk and their coming was the main point of the meeting," he said.
Other delegation members said the meeting paved the way for further talks with Burundi's regime: "We will meet Buyoya again," said Zaire's deputy prime minister Kititwa Tumansi.
The ministers were due to leave Bujumbura for the Tanzanian capital Dar es Salaam after the talks at Burundi's presidency and report back to their respective heads of state.
An earlier plan to include in the talks speaker of the National Assembly Leonce Ngendakumana, a prominent member of the pro-Hutu Frodebu party, was dropped without explanation.
Buyoya's regime, which staged a coup claiming it was the only way to save the country from genocide, has craved recognition from regional neighbours since it came to power.
The regime has been particularly galled by the refusal of neighbouring states to admit it to a series of summits at the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha, government officials said.

Regional states led by Tanzanian mediator Julius Nyerere imposed economic and transport sanctions against Burundi, demanding the restoration of the national assembly, the lifting of the ban on political parties and the start of all-party unconditional talks between the regime and Hutu rebel groups.
Earlier this month the states decided to maintain the blockade, setting a one-month deadline for the start of unconditional talks.
The regime deliberately kept its military presence to a minimum at Bujumbura airport, in an apparent effort to persuade the regional ministers Burundi has returned to civilian rule.
Around 150,000 people have died since October 1993 in Burundi's ethnic civil war, sparked by the assassination of the country's first democratically-elected Hutu president.
The U.N. and regional states have repeatedly warned Burundi could go the way of its northern neighbour Rwanda where up to one million people died in 1994 in a genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
